items.note: Parus borealis de Selys = northern Willow Tit (P. m. borealis), Heligoland. Check.
"Pearls" is a local name. The text glosses it with a query as Tringa ? minuta (Little Stint, Calidris minuta). It isn't settled, so I've kept it at group level.
Name in quotes, from a ship's or light-vessel record. A keeper's identification of a Nearctic vagrant: check.
"Peeve" taken as a form of Peewit/Peewee. Uncertain: check.
"Peeves" taken as a form of Peewit/Peewee. Uncertain: check.
Victorian family heading Pelecanidae covered Cormorant, Shag and Gannet. That is not modern Pelecanidae (pelicans).
Probably storm petrels (Hydrobates pelagicus or H. leucorhous) at lanterns, but it could be Fulmar.
Breeding birds killed by a cat. Almost certainly European Storm Petrel (Hydrobates pelagicus).
Caught against the lantern: probably storm petrels (Hydrobates).
Check that no instance is a "Pewit Gull" (Black-headed Gull).
Victorian subfamily heading. Check whether that section also lists Goldcrests or other warblers.
One is "large, with very conspicuous wing-bar": possibly a Greenish or Arctic Warbler, not identified.
The example ("many... at the Nash on September 3d") reads oddly for Magpie. Check that the name is attached to the right sentence.
"Pie" = Magpie. But check the page: it may be the end of a hyphenated "Sea-Pie" (Eurasian Oystercatcher).
Could be Woodpigeon, Stock Dove, Rock Dove, or homing pigeons at sea.
Could be Woodpigeon, Stock Dove, Rock Dove, or homing pigeons at sea.
Pink-footed or Bean Geese. The text says "probably the former" (Anser brachyrhynchus).
"Pink" = Chaffinch, after its call. Fairly confident.
"Pirr" = Northern Isles name for tern (Arctic Tern there). "Sea Mews" would mean gulls, but arrival on May 26 and departure in September fit terns. Check.
Keepers' "Plover" often means Golden Plover or Lapwing.
"Plover-Knot": perhaps a Red Knot (in summer plumage) or a Grey Plover. Check.
Plover's Page = Dunlin, as glossed by J. A. H. B.
"Pourrin" at the Little Fastnet: about sixty alighted in April. Possibly a form of Purre (Dunlin), but I can't settle it.
Victorian Procellariidae also included storm petrels. Lantern kills are probably storm petrels.
Garbled Procellariidae heading (Victorian sense, including storm petrels).
"Puff": "four shot in summer plumage". Possibly an OCR of Ruff (R→P) or a truncated Puffin. Check the page.
"Purr", the only sea-bird breeding near the station. Taken as Pirr = tern, but Purre is also an old name for Dunlin. Check.
Gätke list "Pusilla, one". If it follows Emberiza it is Little Bunting (Emberiza pusilla). Check the list context.
Gätke's queried Pyrrhula rosea (Pallas's Rosefinch, Carpodacus roseus). Not obtained, and the description (yellowish-green, white wing-band) doesn't confirm it.
Read as Querquedula crecca (Teal). If it were circia it would be Garganey. Check the print.
Budytes raii = Ray's (Yellow) Wagtail, M. f. flavissima.
In a Gätke list, presumably Water Rail.
"rare bird": not identified in the example. Check the surrounding text.
Garble read as RALLIDÆ ("One heard": Corncrake?). Check.
Razorbill and (Common) Guillemot together. You might split this into two records.
Red Linnet = Linnet in breeding plumage.
Red Linnet = Linnet in breeding plumage.
Keeper's name in quotes. Probably Linnet, though a redpoll is possible in December.
Red-breasted Snipe = dowitcher. Shot at Cleethorpes; species not determinable from the name.
Heligoland. Possibly American Robin (T. migratorius) or Red-throated Thrush (T. ruficollis). Check Gätke's text.
Glossed as Choughs in the text.
Keeper's "Red-legged Sandpiper" on deck. Probably Redshank, but Ruff is possible. Check.
Text gives Agelaeus phoeniceus. Probably an escaped cage bird: check before using as a migrant.
Lesser or Mealy not stated. IOC has recently lumped the redpolls, so check your list version: it may be a single species, Acanthis flammea.
"a large Redpoll": probably a Mealy Redpoll (A. flammea).
"Redshank or Sandpiper": the keeper was unsure.
"Redtails (? Redstarts)" stayed from June 3rd to July 2nd. The source queries the identification itself.
"Reed Birds" all day. Perhaps Reed Bunting or reed/sedge warblers; not determinable.
Keepers may have confused this with Sedge Warbler.
The April 4th record is far too early for Reed Warbler and was queried in the source. Probably a misidentification.
Bare "regulus" in a Gätke list, taken as Goldcrest.
Garbled heading. The record is of a "Blackbird" with a white throat.
"Ringnecks (?)". Ringneck is a name for Ringed Plover; Ring-necked Pheasant is also possible. Check the context.
"Robin (Golden-Crested)": the keeper's name for a Goldcrest, not a Robin.
"Rock Birds" leaving Whalsey at the end of August = the breeding auks (guillemots, razorbills). Check.
OCR garble, "five Rock he 6 ae". Possibly Rock Doves or Rock Pipits. Check the page.
Rock Lark = Rock Pipit. "Large flocks" at Sumburgh may include Meadow Pipits.
"Rock Plover" killed at the light. Perhaps Purple Sandpiper or Turnstone; not settled.
"Rock Starling" perched on the lantern: keeper's name. Starling, Ring Ouzel or something else; not determinable.
"Rock Tit" = Rock Pipit (cf. Titlark). Fairly confident.
Listed with Wheatears and Wagtails. Could mean Rock Pipits rather than auks. Check.
Rose Linnet = Linnet in breeding plumage.
OCR: ROSIN = ROBIN (13 observations). Check one page.
Rosy Bullfinch = Pyrrhula rosea. Check the record (one, young). It may be a Common Rosefinch, or relate to Gätke's queried bird (1504).
Some records are queried in the source.
"Royal" Gull: keepers' name. Probably Great Black-backed Gull (see 1664).
Royal Gull: probably Great Black-backed (Larus marinus).
Royal Gull: probably Great Black-backed (Larus marinus).
"Royal or Black-backed Gull": Great or Lesser Black-backed not stated.
Gätke's Anthus rupestris = Scandinavian Rock Pipit (A. p. littoralis).
"Sally-picker" (Irish): Willow Warbler or Chiffchaff, but it is also used for Sedge Warbler.
"Sally-pickers": Willow Warbler or Chiffchaff, or Sedge Warbler.
"Sallypicker (Willow Wren ?)": the source suggests Willow Warbler.
"Sallypickers": Willow Warbler or Chiffchaff, or Sedge Warbler.
"Swallows, Martins, and Sand [Martins]": the name is truncated.
Sand Lark: Ringed Plover ("Sandy Laverock"), Common Sandpiper, or Dunlin/Sanderling, depending on region.
Sand Lark: Ringed Plover, Common Sandpiper, or Dunlin/Sanderling. 75 observations, so worth a regional check.
November 13th is very late. Check the identification.
February records: probably Purple Sandpiper or Dunlin.
Keepers' "Sandpiper" is often Common Sandpiper or Dunlin.
Keepers' "Sandpiper" is often Common Sandpiper or Dunlin. December records are likely Purple Sandpiper or Dunlin.
Gätke's genus Saxicola = wheatears (stonechats were Pratincola). Mostly Northern Wheatear.
Victorian Saxicolinae: wheatears, chats, and possibly redstarts/robins. Check what the heading covers.
"Scar Crows": perhaps Hooded Crow (Irish "Scald Crow") or Black Tern ("Scare-crow"). Check the station and region.
Scart = Cormorant or Shag. They are in different IOC genera (Phalacrocorax and Gulosus), hence family.
Schinz's Sandpiper = small Dunlin (Tringa schinzii Brehm). Some Victorian writers used the name for White-rumped Sandpiper. Keeper's name: check.

notes:
All 350 names in batch4 (n 1400–1749) are mapped: 259 to a species, 52 to a genus or family, 31 to a loose group and 8 as unknown. None was a non-bird.

What to check:
1. Unknown, needing the page: 1476 Pourrin (possibly Purre = Dunlin); 1489 Puff (Ruff or Puffin?); 1501 Pusilla (Little Bunting if it follows Emberiza); 1504 Gätke's queried Pyrrhula rosea; 1621 Ringnecks; 1634 \"Rock he 6 ae\"; 1642 Rock Starling; 1735 Scar Crows (Hooded Crow or Black Tern).
2. Garbles I resolved, worth a glance: 1519 Ratuipm as RALLIDÆ; 1654 Rosin as ROBIN (13 observations); 1452 Pinged Plover as Ringed Plover; 1507 Querquedula \"cracca\" as crecca (Teal) rather than circia (Garganey).
3. Local names I assigned with moderate confidence: Peeve(s) as Lapwing (1409–1410); Pinks as Chaffinch (1455); Pirr, Pirrs/Skirs and Purr as terns (1462, 1463, 1500); Rock Linnets as Twite (1636); Rock Tits and Rock Larks as Rock Pipit (1635, 1643); Red-legged Sandpiper as Redshank (1551); Schinz's Sandpiper as Dunlin (1742); Rosy Bullfinch as Pallas's Rosefinch (1655).
4. Names I left broad because they are ambiguous:
   - Sand Lark (85 observations across 1697–1711): Ringed Plover, Common Sandpiper or Dunlin, depending on region. This is worth settling by station.
   - Sally-picker (1691–1694): Willow Warbler or Chiffchaff, or Sedge Warbler.
   - Royal Gull (53 observations, 1661–1664): left as gulls (Larus), probably Great Black-backed.
   - Rock Birds (1631, 1644): auks or Rock Pipits.
5. Victorian family headings don't match modern families, so I gave them as groups: Pelecanidae (cormorants, shags and gannets) and Procellariidae (which then included storm petrels).
6. Redpolls (1563–1566) are at genus Acanthis. IOC has recently lumped the redpolls, so check your list version: if lumped, these become one species.
7. Records that look doubtful:
   - 1559 Red-winged Blackbird: probably an escaped cage bird.
   - 1584 Reed Warbler on April 4th: too early.
   - 1700 Sand Martin on November 13th: very late.
   - 1438 Pica caudata: the example sentence doesn't fit a Magpie.
   - 1442 Pie: may be a hyphenated \"Sea-Pie\" (Oystercatcher).
8. Keepers' compound names that are also good candidates for splitting into two records: 1526 Razorbill and Guillemot, 1453 Pink-footed or Bean Geese, 1568 Redshank or Sandpiper.

English names follow IOC: Jaeger for Skua, Loon for Diver, Horned Grebe for Slavonian. The British forms are in the notes.
